question: Examine whether the matrix $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$$ can possess an inverse by assuming that a matrix $$B=\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{bmatrix}$$ satisfies $AB=I$, and use the resulting equations to establish whether such a matrix $B$ can exist.
explanation:
Formation of the Product

If $A$ were invertible, there would exist a matrix $B$ of the same order such that $AB=I$. Let $$B=\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{bmatrix}$$ Then $$AB=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}p+2r&q+2s\\2p+4r&2q+4s\end{bmatrix}$$ For $AB$ to equal the identity matrix, we require $$\begin{bmatrix}p+2r&q+2s\\2p+4r&2q+4s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$$

Examination of the Conditions

Equality of corresponding entries gives $p+2r=1$ and $2p+4r=0$. But doubling the first equation gives $2p+4r=2$, whereas the second equation requires $2p+4r=0$. These two conditions are contradictory. Thus no values of $p$ and $r$ can satisfy the required equations simultaneously. Therefore, there cannot exist a matrix $B$ satisfying $AB=I$.

Final Result

Since no matrix $B$ can satisfy the defining condition required for an inverse, the inverse of $A$ does not exist. Hence, $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$$ is not an invertible matrix.

options.C: A matrix $B$ satisfying $AB=I$ exists for infinitely many values of $p,q,r,s$
options.D: No matrix $B$ can satisfy $AB=I$, so $A^{-1}$ does not exist
